Pouring Concrete in Kennewick: Hot Days, Cold Nights, and Getting the Cure Right

Concrete doesn't dry — it cures, through a chemical reaction that needs moisture and moderate temperature. Kennewick is hostile to both. Summer pours face 100°F air, baking sun, single-digit humidity, and wind — a combination that flashes moisture off the surface faster than the slab can hydrate, producing plastic shrinkage cracks in the first hours if the crew doesn't manage it. Winter brings the opposite trap: mild days luring pours that then hit a hard overnight freeze before the concrete gains strength. The best local finishers schedule dawn pours in summer, use evaporation retarders and proper curing compound, and simply refuse marginal winter days.

Then the slab has to live here. The Tri-Cities sees dozens of freeze-thaw cycles each winter — days above freezing, nights below — which is precisely the cycling that spalls weak concrete. Air-entrained mixes, adequate strength specs, and drainage that keeps water from pooling against flatwork all matter more here than in either consistently warm or consistently frozen climates.

Driveways, patios, garage slabs, RV pads (a Tri-Cities staple), steps, and stamped decorative work — we can put you in touch with concrete contractors who pour in this valley year-round and bid it honestly.

Common concrete situations in Kennewick

Surface scaling and spalling on older flatwork

Flaking, pitted driveway surfaces are Kennewick's most common concrete complaint — the legacy of freeze-thaw cycling on non-air-entrained or weakly finished slabs, accelerated by deicer use. Minor scaling can be resurfaced with polymer overlays; deep spalling across a slab is usually replacement territory.

Cracks from soil movement and thirsty roots

The silty soils here shrink hard when they dry, and mature tree roots hunting irrigation moisture lift and crack nearby flatwork. Control joints handle normal shrinkage cracking; slabs cracked by settlement or roots need the cause addressed — compaction, root barriers, or rerouted drainage — or the new slab repeats the failure.

RV pads and driveway extensions built too light

The Tri-Cities loves its RVs and boats, and a pad poured at sidewalk spec (4 inches, light mesh) fails under a 15,000-pound trailer parked all winter. Vehicle pads want 5–6 inches, proper base compaction, and rebar — the cost difference is modest; the durability difference is the whole game.

How it works

  1. 1

    Scope, spec, and site read

    A real bid names thickness, mix strength (PSI), reinforcement, base prep, and joint plan — and accounts for what's under your project: fill, caliche hardpan (common on benches and slopes here), or old slab to demo.

  2. 2

    Forming and base

    Excavation to grade, compacted gravel base, forms, and reinforcement. This invisible half of the job determines whether the visible half cracks — pay attention to compaction talk in bids; the cheap bid usually skips it.

  3. 3

    Pour and finish, timed to weather

    Summer pours start at first light to beat heat and wind; finishing follows the concrete's set, not the clock. Broom finish for traction is standard outdoors; stamped and colored work adds artisan labor.

  4. 4

    Cure, joint, and protect

    Curing compound or wet cure immediately after finishing, control joints cut within hours, and the slab protected from traffic — days for foot traffic, a week-plus for vehicles. In this climate, curing is where good slabs are made and cheap ones quietly ruined.

What concrete costs in Kennewick

Flatwork in the Tri-Cities prices per square foot, climbing with thickness, reinforcement, demo of existing concrete, access difficulty, and decorative finish — plain broom-finish gray is the baseline, exposed aggregate and stamping add half again or more. Small pours carry minimum charges since a crew and truck mobilize either way. Two local notes: demolition and haul-off of old driveway adds real cost (concrete disposal is tonnage-priced), and bids that skip base prep or curing details aren't cheaper — they're just deferring the cost into the slab's short life.

Frequently asked questions

When is the best time of year to pour concrete in Kennewick?

Spring and fall are ideal — moderate temperatures, easier curing. Summer works with a dawn-pour, active-curing crew. Winter pours are possible on mild stretches with blankets and additives, but a forecast freeze within 48 hours of a pour is a reschedule, not a risk worth taking.

Why did my new driveway crack already?

Hairline cracks within control joints' panels usually reflect normal shrinkage — concrete cracks; joints exist to choose where. Cracks that offset vertically, run wild across panels, or appear alongside settling point to base or soil problems. Timing matters too: first-week cracks suggest curing failure in our dry wind.

What PSI concrete should a driveway be here?

4,000 PSI air-entrained mix is the sensible local spec for exterior flatwork — the air entrainment is the freeze-thaw armor. Interior garage slabs can run 3,500. If a bid doesn't specify mix strength and air, ask; the answer tells you about the contractor.

Can my scaling driveway be resurfaced instead of replaced?

If the slab is structurally sound — no major settlement or deep cracking — polymer-modified overlays and resurfacers restore the wear surface at a fraction of replacement cost. Scaling plus heaving, wide cracks, or bad drainage underneath means resurfacing would just re-carpet a failing floor.

Do I need a permit for a driveway or patio in Kennewick?

Patios and flatwork on your own property generally don't need building permits, but driveway work that touches the public right-of-way — new approaches, widened curb cuts — requires city approval. Your contractor should know the line and handle the paperwork when it applies.
